cases.surface_condition: cut splits a numeral token (digits/decimal) on the left from an immediately following scale/unit word on the right (million, billion, percent, %, m, km, inches, meters, etc.)
cases.blamed_rule: - Left or right stretch that ends or begins with a lexical token translators typically render reliably will tend to raise the measured value. Examples of such surface forms: numerals and formatted numbers (e.g., "1,200", "2050"), explicit dates, percentages, currency figures, and short fixed named phrases (e.g., organization names, place names). (Prediction to test: cuts adjacent to numerals/dates often score high.)
cases.proposed_rule: If the token immediately before the marker is a numeral (digits, optionally with decimal/comma) AND the token immediately after the marker is a scale or unit word (examples: million, billion, percent, %, meter(s), m, km, inch(es), lb, kg, etc.), reduce the score into a low band (recommend target band 0–40).

cases.surface_condition: token immediately after the marker is a causal/subordinating connector ('because', 'causing', 'so', 'therefore', etc.) following a quoted/fixed phrase or noun-phrase
cases.blamed_rule: - Cuts before or after subordinators or coordinators can measure well when the segment to the left or right is itself translated reliably (e.g., if the left already ends in a named entity or numeral). Example surface words: "and", "but", "however", "when", "after", "since", "while", "which", "that", "who". Do not assume these always help; the testable prediction is only that presence of reliable lexical material on one side increases measured score.
cases.proposed_rule: If the token immediately after the marker is a causal/subordinating connector (explicitly include 'because', 'causing', 'so', 'therefore', 'hence') — especially when the left ends a quoted phrase or a standalone NP — bias the score downward into a low band (recommend target band 0–30) because the remainder often modifies/overturns the left.

cases.surface_condition: cut splits a numeral token on the left from its unit/scale word on the right (e.g., left ends with '46', right begins with 'percent')
cases.blamed_rule: - Left or right stretch that ends or begins with a lexical token translators typically render reliably will tend to raise the measured value. Examples of such surface forms: numerals and formatted numbers (e.g., "1,200", "2050"), explicit dates, percentages, currency figures, and short fixed named phrases (e.g., organization names, place names). (Prediction to test: cuts adjacent to numerals/dates often score high.)
cases.proposed_rule: If the left token is a numeral and the right token is a unit/scale word (percent/%/million/billion/meter(s)/inch(es)/etc.), penalize the cut (target band 0–40). In other words, do not raise cuts that separate a numeric quantifier from its scale word.

cases.surface_condition: cut separates a numeric token (e.g., '6.34') from the immediately following unit word (inches, m, cm, etc.)
cases.blamed_rule: - Left or right stretch that ends or begins with a lexical token translators typically render reliably will tend to raise the measured value. Examples of such surface forms: numerals and formatted numbers (e.g., "1,200", "2050"), explicit dates, percentages, currency figures, and short fixed named phrases (e.g., organization names, place names). (Prediction to test: cuts adjacent to numerals/dates often score high.)
cases.proposed_rule: When a cut would leave a numeral on one side and its unit/scale word immediately on the other side, lower the predicted score into 0–40 (do not treat an isolated numeral as a reliable single-side unit).

cases.surface_condition: cut immediately after a named organization/place when the right side begins with an appositional parenthetical or abbreviation (right token is '(' or immediately '(' + uppercase abbreviation)
cases.blamed_rule: - Left or right stretch that ends or begins with a lexical token translators typically render reliably will tend to raise the measured value. Examples of such surface forms: numerals and formatted numbers (e.g., "1,200", "2050"), explicit dates, percentages, currency figures, and short fixed named phrases (e.g., organization names, place names). (Prediction to test: cuts adjacent to numerals/dates often score high.)
cases.proposed_rule: Sharpen the named-phrase boost: if a cut follows a named entity but the very next token opens a parenthetical/appositive (e.g., '(' or a comma followed by '(' or an immediate abbreviation like '(MINAE)'), reduce the boost — target band 0–50 — because the parenthetical typically completes/clarifies the name and the remainder often changes meaning.

cases.surface_condition: cut places a numeral on the left while the right begins with the repeated unit word (splitting '378' from 'meters')
cases.blamed_rule: - Left or right stretch that ends or begins with a lexical token translators typically render reliably will tend to raise the measured value. Examples of such surface forms: numerals and formatted numbers (e.g., "1,200", "2050"), explicit dates, percentages, currency figures, and short fixed named phrases (e.g., organization names, place names). (Prediction to test: cuts adjacent to numerals/dates often score high.)
cases.proposed_rule: Treat repeated-unit patterns like numeral on one side + unit token immediately on the other as bad splits; lower score into 0–40. (Same mechanism as the numeral–unit rule above.)

cases.surface_condition: left side ends in an adjectival/participial modifier phrase (e.g., 'most commonly spoken', 'estimated to be', 'reported') that syntactically expects a following noun
cases.blamed_rule: - Cuts that separate two independently meaningful lexical clusters (e.g., noun phrase + independent verb phrase) where both clusters contain content words (nouns, verbs, numerals) and do not leave a dangling single function word are likely to score higher. (Prediction to test: cuts after a main verb or after a multi-word noun phrase with a numeral/name often score high.)
cases.proposed_rule: If the token immediately before the marker is a past participle or adjectival head often used to modify a noun (examples: spoken, reported, estimated, known) possibly preceded by an adverb (e.g., 'most', 'commonly', 'widely') AND the token immediately after is a common noun, lower the score into a middling-to-low band (recommend target band 0–50). This avoids boosting adjectival fragments that lose their noun anchor.

cases.surface_condition: cut breaks inside a named-entity cluster that is followed by a role/noun or parenthetical (e.g., 'alleged Daesh (ISIL) | militant ...')
cases.blamed_rule: - Left or right stretch that ends or begins with a lexical token translators typically render reliably will tend to raise the measured value. Examples of such surface forms: numerals and formatted numbers (e.g., "1,200", "2050"), explicit dates, percentages, currency figures, and short fixed named phrases (e.g., organization names, place names). (Prediction to test: cuts adjacent to numerals/dates often score high.)
cases.proposed_rule: Do not automatically boost cuts that fall inside or immediately after multi-token named-entity clusters when the right side starts a title/role or parenthetical clarification (tokens like '(' or words such as 'militant', 'official', 'president' immediately after). Lower such cuts into 0–50 band unless the right-side chunk is itself a self-contained name/number.

tie_fix: Ties arise when the checklist assigns equal upward and downward biases to adjacent markers (for example both markers are next to numerals/commas or both adjacent to named phrases); add a small deterministic bias (e.g., penalize numeral–unit splits and parenthetical-appositive splits) so they no longer get identical scores.
summary: The prompt systematically over-weights isolated reliable tokens (numerals, short names, commas) and boosts cuts that look locally 'lexical' even when those cuts split numeral+unit pairs, split names from parentheticals/appositives, or leave adjectival/participial fragments that depend on the following noun. Add narrowly scoped negative exceptions: penalize numeral↔unit splits, cuts before causal subordinators (because/causing), and cuts that separate names from immediate parenthetical/appositive material, and lower adjectival fragment endpoints. These targeted adjustments will move scores in the correct direction without removing the useful general tendencies already encoded.
